opus-5.5.text:
Working with physicians has been one of the most clarifying experiences for how I think about scalable oversight. Medicine is a domain where you can see, very concretely, the gap between what a model can produce and what a human can reliably evaluate.

Early on, when we were building and evaluating medical question-answering systems, the natural assumption was that you'd just have doctors grade the outputs and that would be your gold standard. What we found is that it's much messier than that. Physicians disagree with each other quite a bit, especially on long-form answers. A cardiologist and a generalist might rate the same response very differently. And as the models got better, there were more and more cases where a model's answer was arguably as good as or better than what an individual physician would write. At that point the question stops being "is the model right?" and becomes "how do we even know?"

That's essentially the scalable oversight problem showing up in the real world, years ahead of when people expected to hit it in other domains. So a few lessons stood out for me.

First, evaluation design matters enormously. Asking a single expert for a thumbs up or down throws away information. Breaking evaluation into specific axes, like factual accuracy, possible harm, missing information, and alignment with clinical consensus, gives you signal that's much more robust. Pairwise comparisons also tend to beat absolute ratings.

Second, you need to think about the evaluator as part of the system. How much time do they have? What tools can they use? Can they see references or a model's reasoning? Small changes in that setup can shift results more than changes to the model itself. That's a big part of why I think approaches where AI assists the human evaluator, by surfacing evidence, critiquing answers, or flagging uncertainty, are so important. Raw human judgment alone doesn't scale.

Third, and maybe most important, it made me humble about the idea that expert feedback is a fixed ceiling. In medicine you see that the right goal isn't to imitate the average physician. It's to help produce answers that a panel of careful experts, given enough time and support, would endorse. That's a more ambitious target, and it requires better oversight methods, not just more labeling.

So in a way, healthcare has been a preview of where the rest of AI is going. Once models start operating at or beyond expert level, you can't treat human feedback as a simple ground truth anymore. You have to build the infrastructure, both the evaluation protocols and the AI tools that support evaluators, so that oversight keeps pace with capability. Doing that with physicians, where the stakes are real and the expertise is deep, has shaped a lot of my intuitions about how we should approach alignment more broadly.

r001.rationale: The response describes doctors grading medical question-answering outputs and notes that models could produce answers as good as or better than an individual physician’s, presenting this as a real-world scalable oversight problem.

r002.rationale: It mentions answers endorsed by a panel of experts, but does not identify learning from aggregated expert opinions through high-compute reinforcement learning as an approach the team pursued.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because when we started working on medical language models, we very quickly ran into a problem that I think is actually the core problem of scalable oversight in miniature.

When you build a model like Med-PaLM and ask "is this answer good?", you need an evaluator. And the natural thing to do is to go get physicians. But what you discover almost immediately is that physicians disagree with each other. Not on everything, but on a meaningful fraction of cases, two board-certified clinicians will look at the same answer and one will say it's appropriate and the other will flag it as potentially harmful. And these are the experts. These are the people we're supposed to be deferring to.

So you can't just treat the human label as ground truth. You have to start asking: what is the structure of the disagreement? Is it that one of them is wrong? Is it that the question is genuinely underdetermined? Is it that they're weighting different values, like completeness versus brevity, or caution versus actually being useful to the patient? And once you start decomposing it that way, you realize the evaluation problem is itself a research problem. You end up building rubrics, running multiple raters, looking at inter-rater agreement, and being very honest about the places where the ceiling on your evaluation is lower than the ceiling on your model.

The second thing it taught me is that the hard part of oversight is not the cases where the model is obviously wrong. Those are easy. The hard part is when the model produces something that sounds authoritative and fluent, and a reviewer has to actually do the cognitive work to check it, rather than just pattern matching on "this sounds like a doctor." We saw that early on. Answers that were confident and well-written would get rated higher than they deserved, and the errors that slipped through were often subtle: a missed contraindication, a slightly wrong dose range, a reasonable-sounding plan that skipped a step. That's exactly the failure mode people worry about with scalable oversight more generally. As the model gets better than the median evaluator at producing plausible outputs, the evaluator's job gets harder, not easier.

So what did we do about it? A few things that I think generalize. One is decomposition. Instead of asking "is this answer good," you ask twelve narrower questions: does it reflect scientific consensus, is there evidence of incorrect retrieval, is there evidence of incorrect reasoning, is there content that could cause harm, and so on. Narrower questions get you more reliable human judgments and they also tell you where the model is actually failing. Two is using the model to help the evaluator. Having the model surface its reasoning, cite what it's relying on, flag its own uncertainty. That shifts some of the work from "verify this from scratch" to "check these specific claims," which is a much more tractable task for a busy clinician. And three, honestly, is humility about what the evaluation can and can't tell you. We tried to be very careful in the papers about saying this is performance against this rubric with these raters in this setting, not "the model is as good as a doctor."

I think the broader lesson for alignment is that the dream of a clean, perfectly reliable human oracle doesn't exist even in a domain with licensing boards and decades of training. What you have instead is a noisy, expensive, somewhat inconsistent signal, and the research question is how to amplify it. How do you get a group of imperfect experts, plus tools, plus structure, to produce oversight that's better than any one of them alone? Medicine is a nice place to study that because the stakes are real, the experts exist, and you get feedback. And I think if we can't make oversight work there, I'm not sure we should be confident about making it work for systems that are operating in domains where we don't have a hundred years of accumulated clinical judgment to lean on.

r002.rationale: It discusses multiple raters and combining expert judgments, but does not mention learning from aggregated expert opinions through high-compute reinforcement learning or identify that as the team’s approach.

astra-6.text:
Working with physicians has made scalable oversight feel very concrete to me. In medicine, you can’t just ask whether an answer sounds good. You need to know whether it’s supported by the evidence, whether it misses something important, and whether the uncertainty is communicated appropriately. Even for an expert, checking all of that can take a lot of work.

That’s the connection to alignment: generating an answer and evaluating it are different tasks, and we shouldn’t assume that having a human in the loop automatically gives us reliable oversight. We have to give that human the tools and context to make a meaningful judgment.

For example, you could have an AI help surface relevant evidence or identify potential mistakes, while a physician evaluates the clinical reasoning. But then you have to ask whether that assistance actually improves the physician’s judgment, or simply makes the model’s answer more persuasive.

So the lesson I take away is that oversight is a system you have to design and test. The question isn’t just, ‘Did an expert approve this?’ It’s, ‘Under what conditions could that expert catch an error, and do those conditions still hold as the model becomes more capable?’

r001.rationale: The response discusses physician evaluation of AI outputs but does not identify supervision of models that outperform physicians on specific narrow tasks.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention learning from aggregated expert opinions or using high-compute reinforcement learning as Singhal’s team’s approach.

sol-6.1.text:
Working with physicians has made the challenge of oversight much more concrete for me. A doctor can evaluate a medical answer, but doing that carefully can require reviewing a long patient history, checking the evidence, and thinking through alternatives. Expert oversight is valuable, but it’s also expensive and time-consuming.

That raises a central question for scalable oversight: can we use AI to help an expert judge an answer more reliably? A model might organize the relevant information, flag uncertainty, or surface a reason that an apparently convincing answer could be wrong. The physician can then focus their attention on the parts that require their judgment.

The catch is that the assistance itself needs scrutiny. If the model produces a persuasive explanation, that doesn’t necessarily make the answer correct. So I think the important thing to measure is whether the human actually becomes better at distinguishing good answers from bad ones, rather than simply becoming more confident. Medicine makes that distinction especially tangible.
